scenes.tts: A bacterium senses most of its surroundings with two-component systems. Component one is a sensor kinase, usually set in the membrane. When it detects its signal, it takes the end phosphate from ATP. It puts that phosphate on one of its own histidines.
scenes.visual: Membrane bar; a sensor kinase spans it. A signal binds outside. ATP hands its end phosphate to a histidine slot on the sensor.
scenes.narration: A bacterium senses most of its surroundings with two-component systems. Component one is a sensor kinase, usually set in the membrane. When it detects its signal, it takes the end phosphate from ATP. It puts that phosphate on one of its own histidines.

scenes.tts: Component two is the responder. It moves that phosphate onto one of its own aspartates. The change in shape that follows switches it on. Most responders are transcription factors, so the whole pathway is a sensor and a gene switch with one phosphate passed between them.
scenes.visual: The sensor slides left; a responder appears. The phosphate hops to the responder's aspartate slot, its shape changes and it turns on, flipping a gene switch.
scenes.narration: Component two is the responder. It moves that phosphate onto one of its own aspartates. The change in shape that follows switches it on. Most responders are transcription factors, so the whole pathway is a sensor and a gene switch with one phosphate passed between them.

scenes.tts: Set this beside an animal pathway. A phosphate on aspartate is labile. How long it lasts differs from one responder to another, from seconds for Che Y, a swimming responder, to minutes or more for others. A phosphate on serine, threonine or tyrosine stays until a phosphatase removes it. So the cell controls off separately from on.

scenes.visual: Two lanes. Aspartate phosphate: short and long lifetime bars that end. Serine, threonine or tyrosine phosphate: a bar that runs on until a phosphatase cuts it; on and off tags.

scenes.tts: Because that mark stays, another protein can bind it. An S H 2 domain reads a phosphotyrosine. In the bacterial relay, the phosphate changes the responder that carries it, and no separate domain reads it. Most sensor kinases pass their phosphate to one partner and largely ignore the rest. An animal receptor recruits several pathways at once, and each runs through tiers of kinases.

scenes.visual: An SH2 dome closes on a phosphotyrosine; beside it the responder just changes shape and a crossed dome shows no reader. Then one sensor to one partner versus one receptor to several multi-tier pathways.
